direction.treatment: A calm, cinematic journey from the skin's surface into a single pore. Each step of acne formation is a new layer added to one consistent cross-section, so the viewer always knows where they are. Stylised scientific illustration, not gore: no close-ups of real lesions.
direction.style: Dark navy laboratory backdrop, translucent anatomical layers, soft rim light, gentle particle motion.
direction.typography: Inter ExtraBold captions, lower third (y≈1280), keyword highlight in accent cyan; labels as thin-line callouts.
direction.camera: Slow push-ins (2–4% per scene); one iris transition into the pore; no shaking, no whip pans.
direction.transitions: 0.4 s cross-dissolves; iris-in for the surface → inside-the-pore move.
direction.lighting: Cool key from top-left, warm sebum glow, red inflammation bloom as the only hot colour.
direction.sfx: Soft whooshes on transitions, subtle bubble ticks for sebum, low swell for inflammation. No comic SFX.
direction.safety: Illustrations are simplified diagrams; ends with a dermatologist note and an educational disclaimer.

segments.text: Every pimple begins in a place like this. A single pore.
Acne is incredibly common. So what actually goes wrong in there?
Each pore is a hair follicle with an oil gland. The gland makes sebum, and hormones called androgens can push it to make more.
Skin cells lining the follicle should shed and wash out. In acne, they pile up and stick together with the oil, forming a plug.
Inside that plug, a bacterium called Cutibacterium acnes thrives. The surprise? It's the most common bacterium on healthy skin too.
The real trouble is your immune response. Inflammation is what turns a clogged pore into a red, swollen pimple.
So acne isn't caused by dirt. It's oil, clogging, bacteria and inflammation, together. That's why guidelines strongly recommend benzoyl peroxide and topical retinoids.
And if your acne is painful, scarring, or not improving, a dermatologist can help.

claims.text: Acne lesions arise in the pilosebaceous unit (the pore: hair follicle + oil gland).
claims.evidence: Acne is a prevalent inflammatory dermatological condition that predominantly affects the pilosebaceous unit
Acne is a prevalent inflammatory dermatological condition

claims.text: Pores are follicle openings connected to sebaceous (oil) glands that produce sebum.
claims.evidence: The pilosebaceous unit is a metabolically active and immunologically responsive niche composed of sebaceous glands, follicular keratinocytes, lipids, proteins...
androgen hormones, specifically testosterone and Insulin Growth hormone (IGH-1), increase sebum synthesis and secretion

claims.text: In acne, follicle-lining cells are not shed normally and accumulate with lipids, blocking the follicle.
claims.evidence: in acne patients, keratinocytes hyper proliferate and are not shed into the lumen, which leads to the accumulation of irregular desquamated corneocytes in the pilosebaceous follicles coupled with lipids

claims.text: C. acnes thrives in oily, low-oxygen follicles.
claims.evidence: anaerobic, lipophilic, gram-positive ... prefers to colonise in sebaceous follicles because they produce large amounts of sebum and provide excellent anaerobic habitat

claims.text: C. acnes is the most abundant bacterium on (healthy) skin.
claims.evidence: C. acnes is, by far, the most abundant bacterium in the skin microbiota, and its load does not seem to differ between healthy skin and skin affected by acne.

claims.text: The immune/inflammatory response produces red, swollen (inflammatory) lesions.
claims.evidence: when the immune system detects P. acnes, the inflammatory process begins ... These mechanistic processes will produce inflammatory lesions such as ... pustules, nodules, cysts and papules

claims.text: Acne is not caused by poor hygiene or a dirty face.
claims.evidence: Acne is not caused by poor hygiene or having a dirty face (British Association of Dermatologists, Acne Support)

claims.text: Acne involves four interacting factors: excess sebum, follicular hyperkeratinization, C. acnes, and inflammation.
claims.evidence: Acne's pathophysiology involves four important factors: excessive sebum production, hyperkeratinization of pilosebaceous follicles, hyperproliferation of propionibacterium acnes (P. acnes), and inflammation.

claims.text: The AAD 2024 guideline strongly recommends benzoyl peroxide and topical retinoids.
claims.evidence: For patients with acne, the AAD recommends benzoyl peroxide — Strong; ... recommends topical retinoids — Strong (moderate certainty). Benzoyl peroxide to reduce the amount of acne-causing bacteria; topical retinoids to help unclog pores and reduce inflammation.

claims.text: Painful, scarring or persistent acne warrants seeing a dermatologist (general safety guidance).
claims.evidence: Guideline-based management of acne vulgaris is delivered by clinicians; general referral advice, not an individualized recommendation.

titles: How a Pimple Forms, Step by Step
Acne Isn't Caused by Dirt — Here's What Does It
seo.description:
Acne isn't caused by dirty skin. A pimple forms when four things combine inside a pore: excess oil (sebum), clogged follicles, a common skin bacterium called Cutibacterium acnes, and inflammation.

Educational content only — not medical advice. If your acne is painful, scarring or not improving, see a dermatologist.
